Header:
Date: 2026-07-10

Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (HelixAI ML Eng), Luis Martinez (HelixAI SRE), Chen Wei (HelixAI CTO)

Summary:
Brief technical deep dive on per-model tuning strategies for Llama / Mistral / Qwen families. Focus on: runtime performance, latency/throughput tradeoffs, KV cache behavior, batching strategies, quantization impacts, MoE routing costs, and RoPE scaling implications on long-context workloads.

Topics:
- Model-specific kernel choices and quantization profiles
- MoE routing overhead vs sparse compute savings
- RoPE (rotary positional encoding) scale mismatch and fixes for long-context
- VPC / on-prem considerations for Dedicated and Private deployments
- Proposed next steps: benchmarks, load-test, & security doc share

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining we wanted to run through some of the low level tuning knobs we use at Redwood when servicing Llama Mistral and Qwen families and then get into your workload specifics, priya do you wanna kick us off with the perf targets?
[00:18] Priya Rao: yeah thanks alex, so our main thing is 95th p99 latency under 300ms for short responses ~ 128 tokens and then a throughput target of ~120 reqs/sec for chat api in peak, we also have some long context use cases to 32k tokens so rope scaling is a concern.
[00:35] Samir Patel: ok quick note, 300ms at 128 tokens is tight on single-gpu for some larger Qwen L models if you need exact p95 we often recommend either Dedicated with batch piping or model distillation/quantization; we'll run numbers.
[00:52] Luis Martinez: curious about MoE — we like the FLOPS savings on paper but routing overhead plus memory fragmentation scares our infra team, how does redwood account for that?
[01:05] Samir Patel: good question, moes are a tradeoff: routing adds a per-token dispatch cost and extra host-side gather/scatter for experts; for sparse compute you win on raw flops but you may lose on tail latency and memory if experts are imbalanced. our approach: 1) profile routing hot spots with a micro-benchmark, 2) pin experts to contiguous GPU memory to reduce scatter cost, 3) use small-batch routing and fallbacks — and if tail latency matters we suggest hybrid: use dense variant for p95 sensitive traffic and route bulk async workloads to MoE.
[01:40] Chen Wei: any numbers you can share? like routing adds X ms per token?
[01:45] Samir Patel: rough numbers depend on model size and expert count, in our tests for a 70B MoE with 16 experts we saw routing + gather add ~6-12ms per token at small batch sizes, but average token compute savings still produced net throughput gains for high throughput jobs. for p95 focused workloads that 6-12ms matters, so we recommend dedicated pools or client-side batching.
[02:10] Priya Rao: ok that aligns with what we thought. about KV cache — we saw some odd cache invalidation when resizing context windows, any redwood-specific recommendations?
[02:22] Alex Chen: yes KV cache management depends on tokenizer and kv-sharding. two common issues: stale prefix cache when you change the model version or quantization profile, and cache misses when requests jump sequence length. we typically: 1) include a cache key with model version + quantization profile + rope-scale flag, 2) offer automatic prefix trimming for requests that grow beyond configured max seq, and 3) provide telemetry to show cache hit ratio per route in the console.
[02:54] Luis Martinez: telemetry would be great — can we see samples of per-token cache hits?
[02:58] Samir Patel: yes console has token-level breakdowns, we'll share sample graphs in the spreadsheet.
[03:05] Priya Rao: rope scaling — our fine-tuned Llama variant shows degeneration beyond 16k, we tried naive scaling and results were worse. what are redwood's opinions?
[03:18] Samir Patel: RoPE scale mismatch is a common issue. practical fixes: linear rescaling of rotary frequencies, or the ALiBi-style bias, or rewinding tokens with local relative position encodings. for Llama specifically we often apply a rope-correction layer at compile time that shifts high frequency components to mitigate wrap-around. it isn't magic but improves stability for 16k-32k. Mistral and Qwen need per-architecture tuning; Mistral's attention has different norming so the scale factor is different.
[03:52] Chen Wei: are these fixes applied in the runtime or do we need to finetune?
[03:58] Samir Patel: we can apply most as a runtime compile-time transform — it's a kernel-level change that doesn't require full finetune in many cases. for edge cases you may still want a short finetune but often the rope-corrected inference profile is sufficient.
[04:12] Alex Chen: quick interjection: quantization — we've got 4-bit and 8-bit profiles; 4-bit (q4) gives big memory savings but you can see bias on logits for certain sparse heads, so we recommend q8 for p95-sensitive traffic and q4 for background bulk generation.
[04:30] Priya Rao: for q4 do you see more instability on Mistral or Qwen?
[04:34] Samir Patel: Qwen tends to be more sensitive due to its layernorm ordering; Mistral tolerates aggressive quantization slightly better. again, per-model evals in our Optimize toolkit give a delta table for ROUGE/accuracy and hallucination rate by quant profile.
[04:55] Luis Martinez: on VPC/private — we need air-gapped options for compliance. how much of this tuning requires access to redwood control plane? can we run everything on-prem?
[05:08] Alex Chen: Private mode supports an on-prem package; the control plane can be customer-managed. runtime kernels and compile layer run in your VPC. some telemetry can be pushed to your S3/KMS endpoint rather than our metrics store. we'll share the Private deployment whitepaper (link) and SOC/ISO artifacts.
[05:30] Priya Rao: great, you'll send SOC2 and SAML docs?
[05:33] Alex Chen: yup — will attach security deck.
[05:36] Chen Wei: back to batching — what's your guidance for continuous batching vs request-by-request to meet p95?
[05:44] Samir Patel: continuous batching gives throughput wins but increases tail latency variability. for p95-sensitive traffic we suggest small fixed-time windows (e.g., 10-20ms) plus dynamic batch caps, and prefix-aware batching so conversations with long prefix leverage cache hits and avoid re-identifying tokens. on Redwood Dedicated we can tune the batching policy per-route.
[06:08] Priya Rao: about model variants — would you advise using distilled Llama/quantized Qwen as fallback?
[06:15] Alex Chen: yes a multi-tier routing policy often works: primary high-quality model pinned to dedicated pool, fallback smaller/quantized variant in hosted or reserved cheap nodes. automatic fallback keeps service online under capacity pressure. our routing policy can be based on latency SLA or cost thresholds.
[06:32] Luis Martinez: cost modeling — can you demo example of MoE versus dense for our workload?
[06:37] Samir Patel: we'll run a comparative benchmark with your sample prompts. plastered in the spreadsheet we'll include per-token ms, p95, and cost-per-token estimates for dense vs MoE with varying expert counts.
[06:53] Priya Rao: any gotchas on memory fragmentation for MoE on shared GPUs?
[06:57] Samir Patel: shared GPU multi-tenancy plus MoE can fragment memory; we recommend reserved expert allocations or co-locating experts with ample headroom and use of CUDA mempool tuning. Dedicated pools with local expert pinning is the path if you want predictable p95.
[07:16] Chen Wei: fine — for the load test, what config do you need from us?
[07:20] Alex Chen: sample prompt set, expected concurrency curve, target p95/p99 SLOs, and any data residency constraints. also which model variants you want us to include: e.g., Llama-70B dense, Llama-70B-MoE-16, Qwen-60B q8, Mistral-30B q4.
[07:37] Priya Rao: we'll share that by monday.
[07:40] Alex Chen: perfect.
[07:42] -- brief pause / crosstalk --
[08:02] Samir Patel: one more technical note on RoPE: for the long context you asked about, we also add a sliding window KV eviction policy — it keeps hot prefixes in GPU memory and evicts cold tokens to host memory with async fetch. it reduces GPU memory pressure and keeps throughput stable. downside is higher jitter if eviction triggers during a spike.
[08:28] Luis Martinez: sounds reasonable — can we get the telemetery for eviction events?
[08:32] Alex Chen: yes we'll include example telemetry exports.
[08:36] Priya Rao: security follow-up — can you redact logs before they leave our VPC?
[08:40] Alex Chen: with Private you control the telemetry sink; we can apply filters in the agent to redact PII before export. we'll do a short runbook for that.
[08:52] Chen Wei: ok final question — what's typical turnaround for a pilot? we need to move quickly.
[08:58] Alex Chen: from contract to pilot for Dedicated it's usually 2-4 weeks depending on infra approvals; Private on-prem can be 4-8 weeks. for a quick host-run benchmark we can spin up a test job in 3-5 business days.
[09:15] Priya Rao: good.
[09:18] Alex Chen: great, recap of next steps: share spreadsheet + security artifacts, HelixAI share prompt set and SLOs, Samir will do MoE cost doc, Alex to schedule load test. we'll target follow-up meeting next week.
[09:35] Chen Wei: thanks all.
